AMD Showcases 6th Gen AMD EPYC Processors to Lead Next Era of AI and Enterprise Computing :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD Showcases 6th Gen AMD EPYC Processors to Lead Next Era of AI and Enterprise Computing
November 10, 2026 12:00 pm EST
Download as PDF
News Highlights:
6
th
Gen AMD EPYC SP7 CPU-based platforms are now shipping from leading server OEMs and ODMs.
6
th
Gen EPYC CPUs are expected to power cloud instances across all major, global cloud service providers, with recent announcements from Microsoft Azure and OCI showcasing leadership agent orchestration, concurrent agent sandboxes, as well as web and enterprise applications.
Powered by the new AMD “Zen 6” architecture, 6
th
Gen EPYC CPUs deliver a broad portfolio of workload-optimized server CPUs spanning agentic AI, enterprise, cloud computing, HPC and general-purpose computing.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  10, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced the general availability of the 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC™ server SP7 processors, based on the new “Zen 6” architecture, extending its historical server CPU performance leadership as AI creates new demands across the data center. Systems powered by the new CPUs are shipping from leading server vendors, and cloud instances from Microsoft Azure and OCI will be generally available soon.
Across five generations, AMD EPYC processors have repeatedly raised the standard for server CPU performance, energy efficiency and platform choice, culminating in 5
th
Gen AMD EPYC™ processors becoming the fastest-ramping and highest-volume EPYC generation in AMD history. Now, 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC server CPUs extend AMD CPU leadership, running AI agents, accelerated infrastructure and critical enterprise applications, helping customers expand computing capacity that runs their businesses.
More:
AMD Launches 6th Gen AMD EPYC Embedded Processors, Extending CPU Leadership
(News) |
AMD In Depth: EPYC ‘Venice’
(Press Kit, Videos, Photos)
“AI is significantly expanding the role of the CPU across every layer of the data center,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “With 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC, customers can standardize on the proven x86 foundation while choosing a workload-optimized solution to run more agents, keep accelerated infrastructure fed, and power the business-critical applications they depend on.”
World’s Best Server CPU Portfolio for the Modern Data Center
6
th
Gen AMD EPYC is the world’s best server CPU portfolio,
i
providing a workload-optimized stack that delivers leadership performance across a diversity of applications while improving infrastructure economics and preserving the flexibility of the broad x86 ecosystem.
Agentic AI adds even more diversity to a data center as a single workflow can run agents, call models, retrieve data, execute code and interact with the databases and applications enterprises already depend on. The 6
th
Gen AMD EPYC portfolio is designed for that reality, matching CPU density, frequency, bandwidth and efficiency to each job while preserving one common software, security and operational foundation. That workload-optimized approach delivers advantages across critical areas including agentic AI, enterprise services and rack-scale solutions.
Power More Enterprise and Cloud Services:
The 6th Gen AMD EPYC™ 9996 CPU is the world’s best general-purpose processor, delivering leadership performance, performance per CPU watt, performance per CPU dollar and performance per socket. An AMD EPYC 9996 CPU-based system delivers up to 3.7x more performance compared with an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2x the performance and 2.0x the performance per dollar of an Intel® Xeon® 6980P system.
ii
For customers, that can translate into more applications, transactions and users supported by each server, helping create capacity for new workloads within existing data center power and footprint limitations.
Lead Across Every Tier of Agentic AI:
Agentic AI infrastructure spans three distinct CPU roles – general-purpose services, GPU host nodes, and agent sandboxes – and 6th Gen AMD EPYC provides a workload-optimized processor for each. High-frequency host-node processors, with up to 5.3 GHz, can deliver up to 1.8x the LLM output throughput of previous generation EPYC processors
iii
and high-density AMD EPYC processors can provide up to ~3.3x agents-per-CPU-watt advantage over Nvidia Vera and ~2.5x over Intel Xeon 6980P for hosting agent sandboxes.
iv
Additionally, for agent sandboxes, AMD EPYC 9996 CPU-based servers can support an estimated ~1.18x as many agents per rack within the same 35 kilowatt power envelope as systems using default power-management settings.
v
The competitive choice is increasingly straightforward. With 6th Gen AMD EPYC, customers do not have to settle for a one-size-fits-all CPU in a data center that is anything but uniform. AMD EPYC delivers the performance, choice and ecosystem support needed to move AI from answers to action and prepare for what comes next.
From the Server to Rack-Scale AI
6th Gen AMD EPYC extends its leadership from individual servers to AMD Helion™ agentic AI racks, giving customers three deployment options matched to how and where they operate: AMD Helion Liquid, designed to sit side-by-side with AMD Helios™ rackscale solution in large-scale agentic AI deployments, for maximum agent density; AMD Helion Air for expanding agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers; and AMD Helion Air Inference for combining CPU execution and local GPU inference in one rack. AMD has worked across the server ecosystem to help develop the high-density AMD Helion rack with some configurations reaching up to 73,728 threads in one rack, delivering the most agents available in a rack. Customers can choose the balance of CPU and GPU capacity, cooling and connectivity that fits their infrastructure as agent demand grows.
Broad Ecosystem Support and Availability
Systems powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC server processors are shipping from leading server vendors:
Meta
is working with AMD as a lead customer and has been validating 6th Gen AMD EPYC CPU-based platforms as the companies prepare for deployment at scale.
Microsoft
Azure is bringing 6th Gen AMD EPYC to customers across the AI infrastructure stack, with Azure HDv2 now in preview for AI data processing, agentic AI and HPC; Azure HXv2 for EDA and technical computing; and Azure ND MI455X v7, based on AMD Helios, for production-scale AI inference.
AMD recently shared updates to its multigeneration collaboration with
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
(OCI). OCI Compute E7 cloud compute instances will be powered by 6th Gen AMD EPYC server processors, supporting enterprise applications and the CPU services surrounding AI models.
With 6th Gen AMD EPYC, AMD is extending five generations of server CPU leadership into the agentic AI era; delivering more compute, better economics and more choice from the server to the rack. Across enterprise, cloud, HPC and AI infrastructure, EPYC provides a broad portfolio built for the workloads customers run today and what comes next.

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) drives innovation in high-performance and AI computing to solve the world’s most important challenges. AMD EPYC Expands Its Leadership at the Foundation of AI :: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD)
Press Release
AMD EPYC Expands Its Leadership at the Foundation of AI
November 09, 2026 8:00 am EST
Download as PDF
5th Gen AMD EPYC processors power Google Cloud TPU 8tx host infrastructure, helping enterprises protect sensitive AI models
News Highlights:
5th Gen AMD EPYC server CPUs power the host foundation for Google Cloud TPU 8tx, the first cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system with hardware-enforced confidential computing.
AMD EPYC processors enable protection of sensitive AI models and data, combining host processing, security capabilities and x86 software compatibility.
AMD EPYC processors are the host CPU of choice across more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, spanning GPUs and custom AI accelerator ASICs.
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov.  09, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced that 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ processors are powering the host infrastructure for Google Cloud TPU 8tx, the first cloud Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) system to deliver hardware-enforced confidential computing. The expanded collaboration between the companies combines AMD EPYC™ CPU performance, AMD Infinity Guard security capabilities and x86 software compatibility with Google Cloud TPU AI acceleration to help enterprises deploy inference, fine-tuning and reinforcement learning workloads.
1
With Google Cloud’s confidential computing architecture on TPU 8tx supported by 5th Gen AMD EPYC host processors, organizations can run their most sensitive AI workloads at scale in the cloud without compromising on data protection.
The deployment extends the role of AMD EPYC processors as a foundation for accelerated AI infrastructure. Across systems built with GPUs and custom accelerators, AMD EPYC CPUs are the choice for host processing – preparing data, coordinating workloads and managing communication with accelerators. With TPU 8tx, AMD and Google Cloud bring those capabilities together with hardware-rooted security to address a critical requirement for production AI: protecting data while it is in use.
“The most capable AI systems need a CPU foundation that can match the demands of the accelerators they host,” said Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager, Compute and Enterprise AI, AMD. “Across generations of EPYC, we have built leadership capabilities in the performance, memory bandwidth and I/O that keep accelerated systems productive, backed by years of engineering collaboration with the world’s leading cloud providers. Our work with Google Cloud brings that strength to TPU 8tx, helping customers scale AI with the performance and protection their most important workloads demand.”
“When teams move AI agents into production, they need confidence that their data and intellectual property stay private, even from the underlying infrastructure,” said Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager for AI and Computing Infrastructure, Google Cloud. “By pairing 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors with our 8th-generation TPU architecture inside the AI Hypercomputer, we are bringing hardware-enforced confidential computing to cloud TPUs for the first time. Customers get silicon-level data protection alongside the low-latency performance needed for modern reasoning models.”
Enabling Confidential AI with AMD EPYC Processors
In TPU 8tx systems, 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors manage workload orchestration, data preparation and high-throughput communication with TPU accelerators. The system utilizes the AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) capabilities in the AMD EPYC CPU, which together with the TPU, extends confidential computing protection beyond the CPU to connected accelerators, helping protect sensitive data as it moves among them.
Verifying an accelerator’s identity and security configuration before granting it direct access to protected memory helps customer prompts, model weights and intermediate data remain encrypted in CPU memory and in transit among the host and accelerators, with hardware isolation during accelerator execution. These protections help enterprises use sensitive information with confidence in reasoning and agentic AI applications.
AMD EPYC processors also underpin the broader Google Cloud confidential computing portfolio: AMD SEV technologies help protect workloads across Confidential VMs, Confidential GKE, Confidential Space, Confidential Managed Service for Apache Spark, and Confidential Dataflow. TPU 8tx extends that collaboration to confidential AI acceleration.
A Proven Host CPU Foundation Across AI Architectures
As hyperscalers, frontier labs and model providers build increasingly specialized AI infrastructure, CPU selection remains central to system performance and deployment. Accelerators depend on host processors to supply data, schedule work and connect AI workloads with the applications and services around them. AMD EPYC processors are the host CPU of choice for more than 10 leading hyperscalers and frontier AI labs, spanning GPUs and custom AI accelerator ASICs.
AMD EPYC processors support this role across systems using AMD Instinct™ GPUs, Nvidia GPUs and custom silicon. This breadth gives customers a proven CPU platform across accelerator choices, supported by the established x86 software ecosystem.
Building on Generations of AMD and Google Cloud Collaborations
AMD and Google Cloud have collaborated across multiple generations of EPYC processors, supporting general-purpose, compute-intensive, storage-intensive and accelerated workloads leading up to current Google Cloud Compute Engine C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D and G4 virtual machines. The companies have also worked together for years on security technology at the corporate level, including deep reviews of AMD security processor firmware by Google security experts.
With TPU 8tx, this expanded collaboration helps enterprises run modern reasoning and agentic AI workloads in production without compromising on data protection.

Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed initial public offering
Published
Nov 10, 2026
Category
Announcements
Today Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.
The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock.
The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”
The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014.
A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold, nor may offers to buy be accepted, prior to the time the registration statement becomes effective. Today’s announcement does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

Monthly API credits for Max, Ultra, and Team plans
Updated over a week ago
Copy for LLM
Max, Ultra, and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max
$100
Ultra
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max, Ultra, or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max or Ultra:
to be the subscriber
Team:
to be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max or Ultra subscriber, or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max to Ultra.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max or Ultra to Team.
Your Max or Ultra link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max, Ultra, or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge
is a 2B-parameter adaptive reasoning vision-language-action model designed for real-time operation on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor.
The model generates Chain-of-Causation reasoning only when needed and uses a diffusion action expert to produce driving trajectories from surround-camera observations and navigation inputs.
Closed-loop reinforcement learning in
AlpaGym
improves driving performance by 48.9% over the best checkpoint without closed-loop RL.
AlpaJudge
provides human-calibrated evaluation of reasoning quality through reference-based and reference-free variants for different evidence types.
Three workflows connect the edge model with repeatable improvement: running AlpaJudge on PhysicalAI-AV samples, selecting higher-value training examples, and using reasoning scores as rewards for post-training.
Deployment recipes in the
Alpamayo Developer Hub
enable inference optimization with TensorRT and DFlash2, achieving 160-190 ms pixel-to-trajectory latency on DRIVE AGX Thor.
Next Steps
Explore the
Alpamayo 2 Edge model
on Hugging Face to evaluate its capabilities.
Explore the
AlpaJudge model
on Hugging Face for reasoning evaluation.
Visit the
Alpamayo developer forum
for discussions and developer questions.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Autonomous vehicle (AV) developers need reasoning models that can operate within the compute and latency constraints of an onboard system. Larger models provide a foundation for developing these capabilities, but moving them into a vehicle requires additional work to reduce model size, preserve useful reasoning, and validate performance on the target hardware.
NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge
addresses this need with an adaptive reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model designed for real-time operation on
NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor
. Built on the 2B Nemotron-based reasoning backbone of
NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge
and paired with a diffusion action expert, it leverages surround-camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs to generate Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning and future driving trajectories. It reasons
adaptively
, generating reasoning only when needed, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving.
Alpamayo 2 Edge is post-trained with closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL) in NVIDIA
AlpaGym
, improving closed-loop driving performance by 48.9% on top of the best-performing checkpoint without closed-loop RL. Together, these capabilities give developers a strong, edge-ready foundation for bringing reasoning-based driving into an onboard stack.
Making a reasoning model compact enough for onboard deployment introduces a key challenge: preserving the quality of its reasoning and driving behavior as model size is reduced. This requires a way to measure reasoning quality and use that feedback to improve the model. NVIDIA AlpaJudge is the human-calibrated evaluation and reward model used in Alpamayo 2 Edge development to evaluate reasoning traces, select higher-value training data, and provide RL rewards.
This post introduces Alpamayo 2 Edge, explains its inference optimization on DRIVE AGX Thor, and explores three ways to use AlpaJudge in AV development workflows:
Run AlpaJudge-RB and AlpaJudge-RF on a PhysicalAI-AV sample, inspect their scores, and adapt the evaluation to policy-generated reasoning
Select training examples that expose useful learning opportunities
Use human-aligned reasoning scores as rewards for post-training
Together, these workflows connect an edge-oriented driving model with a repeatable process for measuring and improving it.
Bring reasoning-based driving to the edge
An onboard driving model must interpret a changing scene and produce a useful trajectory within the system’s inference budget. The key question is how much driving and reasoning capability a model retains under that constraint.
Figure 1. Alpamayo 2 Edge processes multi-camera video, ego-motion history, and navigation instructions to generate adaptive causal reasoning and driving trajectories, with support for optional visual question answering
To balance model capacity and efficiency, Alpamayo 2 Edge leverages multiple new features:
A 2B-parameter Nemotron-based reasoning backbone, sized for onboard inference
Adaptive reasoning, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving
Offline distillation, training with CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super
Closed-loop reinforcement learning post-training in
AlpaGym
, in which the model learns from the consequences of its actions end-to-end in simulation
Multi-resolution inputs to efficiently encode surround-view observations online
Speculative decoding with
DFlash2
to accelerate online reasoning without sacrificing quality
Recipes for quantization and inference acceleration with NVIDIA TensorRT and NVIDIA TensorRT-Edge-LLM
Figure 2, below, shows how these choices translate into capability, comparing Alpamayo 2 Edge with Qwen-Drive-1.0 across closed-loop driving, open-loop trajectory prediction, and scene understanding and reasoning.
Figure 2. Alpamayo 2 Edge (2B) compared with Qwen-Drive-1.0 (4B) across closed-loop driving, open-loop driving, and scene understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Of note, Alpamayo 2 Edge achieves approximately 60× the distance between at-fault incidents in AlpaSim
Early partner feedback also highlights Alpamayo 2 Edge’s driving performance and inference speed:
“Within days of getting early access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, we had it running closed-loop in NuRec reconstructions of our own London street recordings. In our early simulation tests, Edge kept its lane in more than twice as many runs as Alpamayo 1.5, recovered from lane offsets about 40% more often, and out of the box planned roughly twice as fast as our hand-tuned Alpamayo 1.5 server on the same GPU.”
—
Matas Simonavicius, CTO, PORT
“Alpamayo 2 Edge demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities, reducing displacement error (minADE) by 13.6% and lateral prediction error (RMSE) at 3 seconds by 46.1% compared to Alpamayo 2 Super in our zero-shot evaluation, despite substantial differences in sensor configurations. Fine-tuning on our own driving data delivered a further 44.2% reduction in displacement error compared to the Alpamayo 2 Edge baseline. Within just a few days, we went from receiving the model to running our first tests on a real vehicle.”
—
Luca Crotti, co-founder and motion planning lead, Niulinx
Video 1. Niulinx’s driving demonstration shows the vehicle stopping for a traffic officer’s signal and yielding to pedestrians at a crosswalk
“In less than 48 hours, we made NVIDIA’s Alpamayo 2 Edge run at 10 Hz on AGX Thor for real-time planning.”—
Hans Salomonsson, CEO and co-founder,
Embedl
Video 2. Side-by-side comparison of Alpamayo 2 Edge running in PyTorch and with Embedl optimization, showing differences in planning speed, latency, and reasoning output
The Alpamayo 2 Edge repository’s
inference script
shows how the model operates: It takes in surround-view camera observations over time, navigation text, and historical ego-motion to produce CoC reasoning traces and future trajectories.
import torch
import transformers
from alpamayo2_edge.checkpoint import load_model
from alpamayo2_edge.load_physical_aiavdataset import load_physical_aiavdataset
from alpamayo2_edge.helper import prepare_model_inputs, to_device
from alpamayo2_edge.models.utils import fuse_traj_tokens
data = load_physical_aiavdataset(**clip)
model, loading_info = load_model("nvidia/Alpamayo2-Edge")
settings = dict(
seed=43,
top_p=0.98,
top_k=None,
temperature=0.6,
num_traj_sets=1,
num_traj_samples=1,
max_generation_length=256,
diffusion_kwargs={"inference_step": 10},
)
prepared = prepare_model_inputs(data, model.config, model.tokenizer)
prepared = to_device(prepared, device="cuda")
"""Seed text and diffusion sampling, then run the model on prepared inputs."""
torch.manual_seed(settings["seed"])
generator = torch.Generator(device="cuda").manual_seed(settings["seed"])
with (
torch.inference_mode(),
torch.autocast(
device_type=torch.device("cuda").type,
dtype=model.dtype,
enabled=model.dtype != torch.float32,
),
):
xyz, rot, _, extra = model.sample_trajectories_from_data(
prepared,
num_traj_sets=settings["num_traj_sets"],
num_traj_samples=settings["num_traj_samples"],
top_p=settings["top_p"],
top_k=settings["top_k"],
temperature=settings["temperature"],
max_generation_length=settings["max_generation_length"],
diffusion_kwargs={**settings["diffusion_kwargs"], "generator": generator},
return_extra=True,
)
In particular, note that the model will now produce special
<NOMINAL>
tokens instead of reasoning traces sometimes, indicating routine driving and conserving inference compute.
Retaining quality during deployment
When downloading the model from Hugging Face, by default, Alpamayo 2 Edge’s weights are represented in BF16 and it is directly runnable as a PyTorch model on any supported NVIDIA GPU. To run at real-time on DRIVE AGX Thor, however, Alpamayo 2 Edge must be further inference-optimized.
The
Alpamayo Developer Hub
includes the recipe for the DRIVE AGX Thor deployment workflow: stage the Alpamayo 2 Edge checkpoint and DFlash2 drafter, calibrate FP8 scales, export ONNX graphs, build TensorRT engines with TensorRT Edge-LLM plugins, and run the Python harness. The recipe’s reference configuration was measured on DRIVE AGX Thor-X with DRIVE OS 7.2.7.0, CUDA 13.4, and TensorRT 11.3.1.9.
After following the Alpamayo 2 Edge deployment recipe to stage the model, evaluation inputs, and engines, run the bundle with
python -m alpamayo2edge_edgellm.runtime.run \
--engines "$WORK/engines" \
--model "$MODEL" \
--reference "$INPUTS" \
--dflash2 \
--rolling \
--warmup 1 \
--repeat 5 \
--output "$WORK/results.json"
The recipe documents export, build, calibration provenance, board requirements, and per-stage measurements so developers can reproduce the latency and paired-quality check on their DRIVE AGX Thor configuration. For reference, the resulting optimized model has a pixel-to-trajectory inference latency of 160 ms to 190 ms depending on the amount of reasoning. The same recipe check compares optimized model outputs with a BF16 PyTorch reference built from identical inputs and seeded action noise.
Evaluate reasoning with AlpaJudge
Trajectory metrics describe how a model plans or drives. Reasoning evaluation adds another dimension: whether the model’s explanation identifies the relevant scene context and supports the decision it describes.
AlpaJudge
provides the human-calibrated critic for this aspect of Alpamayo 2 Edge development (as well as prior models). The following workflows describe how to conduct that evaluation and use it for model improvement.
Choose the judge for your available inputs
AlpaJudge provides two checkpoint variants. Choose the variant according to the evidence available for the example you want to evaluate.
Variant
Required inputs
Returned assessment
AlpaJudge-RB, reference-based
Question, reference answer, and candidate answer; no images
One alignment probability in [0, 1]
AlpaJudge-RF, reference-free
Three front-wide and three front-tele frames, ego meta-action history and future, and a candidate rationale
Five rubric probabilities plus action, component, and overall scores
Table 1. AlpaJudge variants use different evidence to assess a candidate rationale
RB measures agreement with the supplied reference, rather than independently checking the scene. RF does not require a reference rationale, but it does require synchronized visual evidence and formatted meta-action context.
Workflow 1: Run AlpaJudge on a PhysicalAI-AV sample
The example notebook
provides a useful starting point, visualizing the data, meta-action context, candidate rationale, and reference rationale tied to a PhysicalAI-AV sample. The same record can then be rescored with a policy-generated CoC trace. Preserve clip ID, timestamp, camera names, and action context in the output so a low score can be traced back to the scene.
In open-loop evaluation, the candidate explanation and trajectory can be compared with recorded annotations. In closed-loop evaluation, the explanation at each policy decision can be scored using the observation and action context from that rollout. A high reasoning score is evidence that a rationale matches the judge’s rubric, while collision, road-departure, close-encounter, and trajectory measures describe different aspects of driving behavior. Report them together.
Step 1: Set up the package and open the notebook
From the AlpaJudge repository root, install the locked environment, authenticate for the model and PhysicalAI-AV dataset, and open the example notebook:
uv sync --locked --dev
hf auth login
uv run jupyter lab examples/alpajudge_pai.ipynb
The notebook uses clip
030c760c-ae38-49aa-9ad8-f5650a545d26
at 5.1 s. It decodes front-wide and front-tele frames at −1.0, −0.5, and 0.0 s, oldest first. The example rationale and meta-action strings are manually authored; the dataset supplies the camera frames. Replace all text fields together when using a different moment.
Figure 3. Visualization of the clip used in the notebook, with multiple camera frames across timesteps shown
Step 2: Download the two judge checkpoints
The notebook downloads
nvidia/alpajudge
once and selects the
reference-based/
and
reference-free/
subfolders. These are separate checkpoints with separate loaders. Its snapshot call filters to those two folders; set
ALPAJUDGE_MODEL_REVISION
to an immutable revision for a reproducible run. A model load needs a CUDA GPU and roughly 5 GB for weights before activations.
checkpoint_root = snapshot_download(
repo_id="nvidia/alpajudge",
revision=MODEL_REVISION,
allow_patterns=["reference-based/*", "reference-free/*"],
)
Step 3: Score the sample and inspect both outputs
Run the notebook’s fixed construction-zone sample first. With its recorded checkpoint and inputs, the smoke test reports RB alignment 0.999 and RF overall 0.842. The five RF subscores assess action/reference agreement, action safety, component grounding, component completeness, and causal consistency. The RF model defines action = p_match × (1 + p_safe)/2 and component = mean(p_grounded, p_complete, p_causal), then combines them overall = 0.6 × action + 0.4 × component.

Agent Substrate
multiplexes many agent sessions over a small pool of warm Kubernetes worker Pods, checkpointing idle sessions with full memory and filesystem state and restoring them onto any free worker.
The runtime targets three workload types: coding assistants that alternate between LLM calls and repository operations, reinforcement learning post-training with bursty CPU-heavy environments, and short-lived GPU sandboxes for research compilation and benchmarking.
Upstream contributions include request parking in the router to queue turns when all workers are busy, per-container resource limits for microVM sandboxes, and a vendor-neutral design for pausing and restoring GPU state using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation.
NVIDIA Dynamo
coordinates inference across GPU workers while Agent Substrate manages agent environments, with Dynamo's router using session identity, KV cache location, and tool-call boundaries to keep related model calls on workers that already hold reusable context.
Dynamo exposes inference signals such as projected time to first token and GPU-pool saturation back to Agent Substrate, which uses them to decide whether to keep an actor resident, suspend it during long inference waits, or resume it as the model response nears completion.
KAI Scheduler places the Substrate worker Pods alongside GPU trainers and inference servers, and the combined stack runs on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform with Substrate as an independent CNCF Sandbox project integrating with DSX OS components.

AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per session holds memory for sessions that aren’t doing anything, and deleting Pods between turns pays a multi-second cold start every time and loses the agent’s state. RL post-training hits the same wall.
Agent Substrate, now donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, is an open-source, security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. It multiplexes many sessions over a small pool of worker Pods. Idle sessions are checkpointed, memory and filesystem included, and restored onto whichever worker is free when the next request arrives. As agentic infrastructure fragments into proprietary runtimes that bypass Kubernetes, NVIDIA is contributing upstream to keep this work open.
This post covers which workloads suit Agent Substrate, what is being built upstream, and how the project works with KAI Scheduler and NVIDIA Dynamo components in the
DSX AI Factory Platform
.
The shape of an agent workload
Traditional web services run as a relatively small number of long-lived instances.
Agents
follow a different pattern: they wake up and take one step, running a shell command, editing a file, calling a test suite or calling an LLM. Then they wait, sometimes for milliseconds and sometimes for minutes, before the next step. The agent’s state (its filesystem, its processes, its working directory) has to continue  between steps.
Kubernetes struggles because spinning up a compute Pod for an agent means a trip through the API server, admission, etcd, the scheduler, the kubelet, image pulls and network setup. That takes seconds, which is fine for a service that runs for weeks. It’s far too slow for a sandbox that must appear, run a 10 ms bash command and get out of the way, hundreds of times per second.
This leaves platform teams with two suboptimal choices: either keep one Pod warm per agent and pay for compute that is idle almost all the time, or create Pods on demand and pay a cold start penalty on every step.
How Agent Substrate works
Agent Substrate uses Kubernetes for running a pool of ready pods. It creates a separate control plane that maps a large set of actors (agents and their environments) onto that smaller pool of workers. When an actor goes idle, it is snapshotted out of its sandbox (gVisor or a microVM) and its worker is freed. When the actor is called again, it is restored into whichever worker is free, with its memory and filesystem state intact.
Waking an actor doesn’t require a new trip through the API server, scheduler or kubelet. Agent Substrate restores the actor onto an existing worker instead. The worker pods are still ordinary Kubernetes Pods, so cluster scheduling, quotas and placement policies still apply as we describe later.
The use cases driving demand
We see three kinds of workload driving demand for Agent Substrate:
Coding assistants and agent serving:
A coding agent alternates between LLM calls and work in its own environment: cloning a repository, editing files, running builds and tests. Users expect the environment to persist between turns and to respond immediately. A platform serving thousands of these sessions can’t afford a dedicated warm sandbox for each one.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training with agentic environments:
RL with verifiable rewards runs GPU trainers and generation servers alongside a fleet of CPU-heavy environments (code sandboxes, compilers, browsers, simulators) that execute actions and check results. Sandbox demand arrives in bursts as rollout batches dispatch actions. A training run can grow from a few hundred sandboxes in early experiments to many hundreds of thousands in production. The slowest environment determines when the trainer gets its next batch, so cold starts on that path leave GPUs idle.
GPU sandboxes for research:
A researcher’s coding agent needs a GPU, not to serve a model but to compile CUDA code, benchmark a kernel or run a numerical calculation. It launches a GPU sandbox on a shared cluster, runs the job and deletes the sandbox. Supporting this across an organization requires many short-lived, isolated GPU sandboxes that start quickly and share a limited pool of GPUs fairly.
Upstream work: What’s landed and what’s next
Each contribution below started from one of those use cases. All of this work is public in the
Agent Substrate repository
:
When every worker is busy, the next request waits instead of failing:
In an oversubscribed system, such as a coding-assistant platform at peak or an RL rollout burst, a user’s next turn can arrive while every worker is busy. Agent Substrate used to return an error immediately, even though another actor would usually free a worker a moment later.
Request parking in the Agent Substrate router (
#221
) holds the request and retries the resume until a worker frees up, with a bounded wait and a cap on how many requests can wait at once. A follow-up (
#1229
) makes sure requests to already-running actors never get stuck in that line.
Giving agents a GPU inside their sandbox:
The research GPU sandbox described above, along with GPU-backed RL environments such as simulators.
We are working on device-pluggability that adds device support on Kubernetes
Dynamic Resource Allocation
(DRA). Device vendors plug in their devices through a profile, each container in a sandbox requests only the devices it needs (
#752
), and the same model works for both gVisor and microVM sandboxes. NVIDIA GPUs will be the first supported device.
One container can’t starve or kill its neighbors:
An agent sandbox often runs the agent’s workload next to helper containers for logging, proxying or metrics. Some of those may be untrusted. A runaway container shouldn’t consume the whole sandbox’s memory and take the agent down with it.
Per-container CPU and memory limits for microVM sandboxes (
#859
) addresses that issue. A container that exceeds its memory limit is stopped on its own, and the rest of the sandbox keeps running.
Preserving GPU sandboxes across suspend and resume
When an agent pauses to wait for human review, its sandbox should release the GPU and resume later with its compiled artifacts and loaded data still in place. Supporting that requires saving and restoring both the agent’s state and the GPU state.
Restoring GPU state introduces hardware compatibility constraints. A GPU checkpoint can usually be restored only onto the same GPU model, and sometimes only with the same driver version. Agent Substrate proposes a design to address this.
Device vendors describe how to pause their devices safely and which device properties a snapshot depends on. Agent Substrate records those properties with each snapshot and restores the sandbox on a matching device, or falls back to a clean cold start if none is available. The design is vendor-neutral and builds on DRA. NVIDIA GPUs are the first target; the design can be extended to other hardware types.
NVIDIA Dynamo: Connecting the agent loop to the inference loop
Agent Substrate manages where agents act; inference runtimes manage where they think. Both face a similar efficiency challenge: keeping idle sandboxes warm wastes CPU and memory, while rebuilding model context on repeated model calls wastes GPU cycles. Scaling each layer independently improves utilization. Coordinating them can also reduce latency and preserve reusable context as agents move between tool execution and model calls.
NVIDIA Dynamo
, the open-source distributed inference framework, provides that coordination. Agent Substrate activates, suspends and restores stateful agent environments across a pool of warm sandbox workers. Dynamo orchestrates inference across GPU workers. The Dynamo router sits between them and connects what the agent is doing with what is happening on the GPUs.
Making inference agent-aware
Traditional inference routing treats every model call as an independent request. In an agent, each request is one step in a longer loop, and consecutive requests often reuse the same system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history and earlier observations.
Dynamo’s router sees where reusable key-value (KV) cache lives, which workers are busy with prefill or decode, and how load is spread across the GPU fleet. Agent Substrate and the agent harness add signals such as session identity, request priority, expected output length, tool-call boundaries and lifecycle events.
With both, Dynamo can:
Keep related model calls on workers that already hold reusable KV cache, without creating overloaded GPU hot spots
Prioritize interactive turns over background agent work when the inference pool is under pressure
Keep system prompts, tool definitions and conversation history available across tool-call gaps
Drop cache state from terminated subagents, closed reasoning branches or summarized contexts first
Prepare likely context as a tool call approaches completion
Feeding GPU intelligence back to Agent Substrate
The most important part of the integration is that Dynamo exposes inference signals to Agent Substrate, helping it decide when to keep agents running, suspend them or resume them.
Dynamo is closer to GPU execution than the agent runtime. It has visibility into cache readiness, queue pressure, active prefill and decode work, and how long an LLM request is likely to take. That information can inform both inference routing and how Agent Substrate schedules agent sandboxes.
Dynamo can return signals such as projected time to first token, projected completion time, request progress, cache readiness, and GPU-pool saturation. Agent Substrate can use this feedback to decide whether to keep an Actor resident, suspend it during a longer inference wait, or resume it as the model response approaches completion.
At fleet scale, the same feedback can help tune warm-worker capacity, regulate agent and subagent fan-out, and avoid activating CPU sandboxes that would otherwise sit idle behind a saturated GPU queue.
This integration establishes a simple division of responsibility. Agent Substrate manages the high-frequency lifecycle of agent environments. Dynamo manages the high-performance lifecycle of inference. Dynamo connects the two around the loop that defines agentic computing: model call, tool call, observation, and model call again.

Agent Substrate is still evolving. Its APIs are still changing, GPU support is being rebuilt on the new DRA foundation, and parts of the Dynamo agent integration are experimental. Now is a good time to contribute and help shape the core design.
Running Agent Substrate with KAI Scheduler and Dynamo
Agent Substrate runs above Kubernetes and works alongside the NVIDIA software that serves models and places workloads. Substrate manages stateful agent environments,
KAI Scheduler
places the Kubernetes workloads, and Dynamo serves the models and exchanges inference-state signals with the agent runtime.

On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Google AI Edge Team
Android ML Team
Share

Today, we are introducing
on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR)
and
Text-to-Speech (TTS)
capabilities in
Google AI Edge Gallery
. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate,
multilingual ASR
and
expressive TTS
models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.
This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:
Android: faster, more accurate system speech models with ML Kit:
Powered by Google’s latest on-device speech models, ML Kit delivers incredibly accurate multilingual transcription across 100+ languages at 10x real-time speed. It is paired with a few-step diffusion TTS model that begins speaking in just ~100 ms and synthesizes 24 kHz audio at up to 50x real-time speed. Both models are integrated into the OS, adding 0 MB to your APK.
Web, Desktop and Beyond: cross-platform, open-weight speech with MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT:
For cross-platform apps, we optimized new .litertlm model speech bundles, including Parakeet-TDT 0.6B, PocketTTS 100M, Kokoro-82M, and Phonon 31M. They deliver real-time streaming transcription and low-latency speech synthesis in a compact memory footprint, and run smoothly alongside on-device SLMs without compute contention.
Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new
XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher
showcase, upgrades
AI Chat
in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.
Multimodal voice tutoring with XR Language Teacher
Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together
100% locally on your phone
with no network connection needed, we built the
XR Language Teacher
showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask
"What is that, and how do I ask for one?"
, and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
Seeing, speaking, and learning entirely on device
Live visual grounding and streaming voice input:
Point your camera at a street sign, menu, or object and ask a question aloud. On-device ASR streams your spoken question in real time alongside the camera frame to
Gemini Nano
on Android devices —or
Gemma 4
across other platforms—in a single pass.
Structured outputs for bilingual TTS code-switching:
Using a structured output schema, the model explains the scene in your own language while tagging foreign-language phrases separately, allowing the TTS pipeline to seamlessly switch voices and accents mid-sentence from your mother tongue to the target language alongside an on-screen vocabulary card.
Adapt for intelligent eyewear
With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at
Android Dev Summit:
Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano
.
Streaming voice dictation and read-aloud playback in AI Chat
Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main
AI Chat
feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
Video of AI Chat Voice input + output
Sentence-synchronized playback and configurable speech settings
ASR and TTS settings in Model Management:
Choose between available ASR and TTS pipelines, preset voices, and downloaded language packs in one central place.
Read-aloud playback with live sentence highlighting:
Turn on “Auto-play TTS” or tap the speaker button on any response to launch a floating TTS bar that highlights each spoken sentence in real time, with the ability to jump to any sentence by tapping it.
Reference implementation for chat voice outputs:
Our open-source codebase demonstrates how to strip Markdown syntax, skip non-spoken blocks like code snippets and tables, and schedule synthesis at the sentence level to avoid compute and memory contention during LLM token generation.
Under the Hood: Building with ML Kit, MediaPipe Tasks, and LiteRT
While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our
open-source code on GitHub
shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using
ML Kit
, as well as
MediaPipe Tasks
and
LiteRT
for cross-platform coverage and open model support.
Building for flagship Android with ML Kit
For developers building for Android devices,
ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs
provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through
AICore
and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.
ML Kit GenAI Speech Recognition API
:
Streams live partial and final transcriptions as the user speaks, accepting audio from either the built-in device microphone or external audio streams such as smart glasses. Our latest on-device ASR advancements deliver incredibly accurate multilingual recognition across 100+ languages (reaching 8.0% to 9.0% Word Error Rate on FLEURS) while transcribing speech 10x faster than the real time audio being transcribed (~300 ms per 3 seconds of speech) and cutting end-to-end speech translation wait times by 35% to 44%.
ML Kit GenAI Text-to-Speech API
:
Powered by a compact, few-step diffusion model accelerated on NPU, the on-device TTS begins speaking in ~100 ms and generates natural 24 kHz speech across 8 expressive voices and 21 locales at up to 50x real-time speed. It synthesizes a 27-second paragraph in just ~500 ms while cutting active device power by over 50% compared to traditional autoregressive TTS models, and includes built-in earcon support.
Building across platforms with MediaPipe Tasks
Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines.
MediaPipe Task
simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:
MediaPipe Speech Recognition (ASR) Task
:
Automatically handles audio framing, configurable Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and decoding. It supports real-time streaming, full-sentence batch, and hybrid transcription modes (streaming live words as the user speaks and refining the full sentence once speech ends), and showcases open-weight models like
Parakeet-TDT 0.6B
out of the box.
Try it now
directly in the browser!
MediaPipe Text-to-Speech (TTS) Task
:
Provides a turnkey synthesis interface with voice selection and low-latency streaming audio output, showcasing open-weight models out of the box, including multilingual models like
PocketTTS 100M
and
Kokoro-82M
, as well as ultra-lightweight English models like
Phonon 31M
with sub-100ms Time-to-First-Audio (TTFA) on most devices and platforms.
Try it now
directly in the browser!
Powering cross-platform speech and flexible model support with LiteRT
Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by
LiteRT
, Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.
Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including
Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3
(multilingual ASR),
PocketTTS 100M
(multilingual TTS),
Phonon 31M
(ultra-lightweight English TTS), and
Kokoro-82M
(multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant
Hugging Face LiteRT Community
with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of
multimodal model examples
to help you get started, with more on the way.
Get started today
Adding a local voice pipeline takes on-device SLMs beyond typing-based chat interfaces, enabling natural, voice-first interactions that work anywhere, completely offline. All the building blocks to try these experiences or integrate them into your own apps are available today:

What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
- Google Developers Blog
What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
NOV. 9, 2026
Sujeeth Jinesh
Software Engineer
Shaurya Gupta
Software Engineer
Luke Baumann

Monica Song
Product Manager

AI Developer Relations

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
TLDR
Today, we announce the General Availability of
Pathways on Google Cloud Platform
. In this post, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. We discuss how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.
Most large-model training runs as Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) programs. Every accelerator runs the same program in lockstep and coordinates through collectives like AllReduce.
It works well when your job is the same program running on every device. It struggles when the job is no longer uniform, like a pipeline whose stages wait on each other or an RL loop where a sampler, a reward model, and a trainer are different programs that have to overlap.
Large runs also have to survive hardware failures, which interrupted
Gemini 2.5 training multiple times per hour
. In SPMD, one lost machine stops every process and sends the run back to its last checkpoint. In each case, the challenge is coordination. You have to decide what runs where and in what order, how tensors move between devices, and how the job keeps going when a machine drops out.
In this post of the series “Pathways on Google Cloud”, you will learn about Pathways, the distributed system Google built to train its own large models, including Gemini. The post discusses how Pathways addresses the coordination challenge by introducing one client that describes the whole computation as a graph, and how the distributed runtime places it, moves the tensors, and keeps the accelerators busy.
By the end, you'll know where SPMD is suboptimal, what single-controller execution changes, and how Pathways coordinates a whole training job across a cluster.
When scaling becomes a coordination problem
If you train PyTorch models, you almost certainly use
Distributed Data Parallel (DDP)
or
Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)
. DDP runs a copy of your script on every accelerator and averages gradients with a collective operation such as AllReduce. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers so that the model fits at all.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 1: One training step with DDP and with FSDP.
DDP and FSDP both follow the Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) execution model. Every process runs the same copy of your script, owns its accelerators for the whole run, and moves in lockstep with the others, because the only way they coordinate is through collectives like AllReduce. Inside one tightly connected group of accelerators those collectives run over a fast interconnect and are cheap. Scale the job across groups and the same collectives cross the datacenter network, which is far slower. On a
TPU v5p
, for example, each chip gets 1,200 GB/s of bidirectional chip-to-chip bandwidth inside its group, but only 50 Gb/s (gigabits, about 6 GB/s) to the datacenter network which is roughly two orders of magnitude less.
And because every step blocks on its collectives, that communication lands directly in step time. The more groups you span, the larger the share of each step spent moving data, so throughput grows slower than the number of accelerators you add.
As long as your training job is one program that fills the hardware you give it, this execution model fits well. You write your model as if there were one device, and the collectives do the rest. But fitting a model into memory is only part of the problem. Keeping every accelerator busy is the harder part, and this is where the SPMD model starts to show its limits.
Take
pipeline parallelism
as an example. You split a model into blocks across devices, and each device now runs different code over smaller micro-batches. Activations flow forward, activation gradients flow back, and while device 0 works on the first micro-batch, devices 1 and 2 wait. Apart from the idle accelerators you keep paying for, this drops utilization and throughput, even though every device has work in the steady state.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 2: Three devices, four micro-batches. The hatched slots are the pipeline bubble.
Another example is RL post-training for an LLM. You have a sampler that generates rollouts, a reward model that scores them, and a trainer that updates the policy and sends the new weights back to the sampler. These are three different programs that should overlap; otherwise the sampler is idle while the trainer runs, and the trainer is idle while the sampler generates.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 3: The same RL loop, run one after another and overlapped (toy schedule).
In both scenarios, the job is now several different programs running on different devices, and their dependencies can no longer be managed through a single collective. You now have to coordinate which devices share which tensors, which processes run while others are still finishing, and how early to enqueue the next buffer so an accelerator never waits for input. Because each worker only has visibility into its local devices and data, no individual process can manage all of these dependencies itself. That has several consequences.
First, because each process owns its accelerators for the whole run and every collective blocks until all devices finish, one failed machine prevents the collective from completing and stops the entire job, forcing a restart from the last checkpoint. You cannot add devices mid-run, and you cannot give devices back.
Second, because each process holds its accelerators from start to finish, capacity can't move to where it's needed. Within one job, a stage that needs fewer chips than another still keeps the extra ones. They sit idle, you keep paying for them, and no other part of the job can use them until the run ends. Across a team, the same happens at cluster scale. Every job owns its accelerators for as long as it runs, so sharing a cluster means splitting it into per-job allocations, and each new job brings up its own processes on its own hosts.
Finally, the development process itself gets harder. On one host you iterate fast because you run the script, drop into a Python shell, set a breakpoint, and debug. This is not true once the job spans many hosts. You need a launcher to push your script to every host, you hit coordination bugs that never showed up on one machine, and there's no single process to break into. When something hangs, each worker is stuck at a collective waiting for the others, with no one place that shows the whole job.
So the common challenge here is the coordination itself. As soon as the job stops being one program in lockstep, you have to decide what runs where, in what order, and how tensors get from one device to the next.
One way to describe this is as a graph, where each block is a node, each tensor that moves between blocks is an edge, and the devices are where the nodes are placed. You can wire that graph up by hand in SPMD, one process at a time. But what if a single client declared that graph, including what each block does, what it needs, and where it runs, and a distributed runtime handled the transfers, dependencies, and ordering along its edges?
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 3: The same RL loop, run one after another and overlapped (toy schedule).
That is the idea behind
Pathways
, the distributed system Google built to train its own largest models, including Gemini. Pathways runs
JAX
programs on
TPUs
and it is
available on Google Cloud
.
Coordinating the entire computation with Pathways
With Pathways, you define the end-to-end computation from a single Python client, without writing custom coordination code, and a distributed runtime executes it. That client is decoupled from the hardware. It runs on an ordinary CPU machine and you write your program against virtual devices; a resource manager maps them onto real chips, and a worker on each accelerator host runs the compiled programs it receives.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 5: Virtual devices, the resource manager, and a remap after a host failure.
Because your code refers to virtual devices rather than physical ones, the runtime is flexible to allow users to change the devices used for a given computation. This allows you to stay in control while the runtime handles the mapping to hardware. In an RL loop, for example, the trainer and the samplers rarely want the same number of chips, so you can give the sampler stage more chips by asking for more virtual devices.
Also, the same capability helps when a host fails or the hardware isn't ready yet. If a host dies, the resource manager remaps the work onto healthy chips and the run keeps going instead of relaunching the whole job, which is the basis for
elastic training
. And because the program targets virtual devices, compilation can start before the physical chips are provisioned, so setup overlaps with provisioning instead of waiting on it.
The resource manager owning the chips also means one Pathways cluster can serve several clients, so researchers on a team can share its capacity. With the
Shared Pathways Service
, the cluster stays up as a long running service, which lets you develop interactively on TPUs hosted on GKE. Each client connects on demand from a laptop or VM, gets its own slices (groups of tightly connected TPU chips) from the shared pool, and hands them back when it disconnects. When every chip is busy, the next workload waits until capacity frees up.
Take the three-block model from Figure 2. Block A runs on one group of devices, block B on a second, block C on a third. You declare what each block computes, its target devices, and where its outputs go. Pathways expresses those dependencies as a distributed dataflow graph, in which each block is a compiled SPMD program and each edge is a tensor the runtime has to deliver.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 6: The distributed dataflow graph. Solid arrows cross groups; dashed edges stay local.
In a single SPMD program, the framework handles the collectives that keep the devices in sync within a group, with or without Pathways, and your code doesn't change. The difference shows up once the job runs several programs on different groups (Multiple Programs, Multiple Data, MPMD), like these three blocks or the sampler, reward model, and trainer of an RL loop. Then no single process sees both sides (the same limit from before, where each worker only knows its own devices), so getting a tensor from block A to block B is a hand-off you have to coordinate yourself.
Pathways closes that gap. You declare the dependency once, and the runtime moves and reshards the tensor for you, over the fast interconnect within a group and over the datacenter network between groups.
To keep the accelerators busy, Pathways prepares launches ahead of time with futures and parallel asynchronous dispatch. While block A is still computing, block B can't run yet, but its input shapes and dtypes are already known, so the runtime allocates B's buffers and schedules the transfer before A's output even exists. Host-side setup for every block happens up front, and each block launches when its inputs arrive.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 7: Sequential setup versus asynchronous dispatch (illustrative durations).
This is also what keeps the single client from becoming a bottleneck. Because dispatch is asynchronous, the coordination work overlaps with the compute already running on the chips, so the client stays off the critical path instead of stalling the accelerators between steps.
In Pathways, the runtime decides execution order when a group has more than one operation ready. In pipelined training, B's devices often hold both the forward pass for an upcoming micro-batch and the backward pass for an earlier one. If each device picked on its own, their collectives would conflict and the group would stall.
Pathways has a central scheduler that puts every program's operations into one consistent order, so operations that must communicate start together instead of deadlocking.
Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video
Figure 8: Without a shared order the group stalls; with one scheduler it keeps moving.
And because it's still one client, the development loop we mentioned before comes back. It's the same single Python process whether you drive one host or thousands of hosts, so you can
drop into a shell
, set a breakpoint, and inspect the run as it goes. When something stalls, there's one place that knows what's queued on every device and which dependency hasn't been met, instead of a hang spread across separate processes.
Put together, Pathways separates model building from execution. You choose how the model partitions across hardware using the client. And the runtime handles the transfers, ordering, and scheduling that keep accelerators busy, across the whole cluster rather than just your slice of it.
Described this way, Pathways can start to sound like an orchestrator you already know. If scheduling work, moving tensors, and keeping a whole cluster busy brings Ray to mind, it should. But the two work at different layers.
Isn't this what Ray does?
Ray
is an open-source framework for orchestrating Python-native AI workloads across large clusters. It provisions the cluster, schedules your Python code as
tasks and actors
, and launches your workload across hosts, holding data loading, training, serving, and tuning under one control plane. To Ray, an accelerator is a resource to schedule.
What Ray doesn't change is how your training runs on the chips. The job inside each worker
still runs as SPMD
. The framework inserts the collectives, and each process sees only its own devices. Ray places and starts that job but it doesn't turn it into a single program that drives the whole cluster.
That is the layer Pathways works at. It changes the execution model underneath, so one client coordinates every chip. Because they sit at different layers, the two are complementary. In principle, Ray can orchestrate the cluster and the pipeline while Pathways handles how the training step executes.
So concretely, Ray's job is about orchestration while Pathways' job is about execution. With Ray, you tie your data, training, serving, and tuning together and spread heterogeneous work across accelerators and clouds. With Pathways, you run one model across many groups of chips, express patterns beyond SPMD, and recover from a failed host instead of relaunching the whole job.
Conclusion and next steps
When a training job stops being one uniform program, the challenge becomes coordinating the dependencies between stages, the tensors that cross the network, and the ordering that keeps every accelerator fed.
SPMD requires you to address these dependencies. With Pathways, you describe the computation once, from a single client, as a graph of blocks and the tensors between them. And you have a runtime that places the blocks on virtual devices, moves and reshards the tensors, orders the work across the cluster, and remaps around a failed host.
With Pathways, model building and execution are separated and you reason about the whole cluster instead of one slice of it.
If you are curious to learn more about Pathways, you can take a look at the following resources:
Pathways on Google Cloud -
Documentation
Pathways: Asynchronous Distributed Dataflow for ML -
Paper
Resilient training with Pathways -
